---
title: "Testing"
description: "How tests are laid out, configured, written, and run."
---

Every project is tested with **pytest**, configured in `pyproject.toml` and run through
`make test`, locally and in CI. The subsections below describe how tests are laid out, configured,
written, and run.

Most of these practices are shared across the projects. A few are marked **(new)**: they're
established in this example repository and are being adopted going forward, so older projects
don't follow them yet.

## 11.1 Layout and naming
- Tests live in a top-level `tests/` folder, outside the package, so they never ship in the
  wheel.
- **One test file per module (new).** The tests for `mypkg/_formats.py` live in
  `tests/test_formats.py`, so the tests for any piece of code are easy to find, and a new module
  gets a new test file. The leading underscore of a private module is dropped: it tells users
  "not public API", and tests don't need it. (Existing projects mostly follow this already, but
  great-tables and pointblank also have some `test__utils.py`-style names, and whittaker groups
  some tests by feature.)
- Large modules can split their tests by topic with a shared prefix: `test_formats_dates.py`,
  `test_formats_numbers.py`.
- `tests/test_package.py` covers the package as a whole rather than one module: `__version__`,
  and that `__all__` matches the intended public API (see 11.11).
- Shared fixtures go in `tests/conftest.py`. Data files the tests read (CSV inputs, reference
  output from R) go in `tests/fixtures/`. Snapshot files are kept in `tests/__snapshots__/` (or
  `tests/snapshots/` with pytest-snapshot) and committed.
- When tests need shared helper functions, `tests/` gets an `__init__.py` so they can be imported
  as `from tests.utils import ...` (as in great-tables).
- Test names describe the behavior being checked (`test_fmt_currency_unknown_code`), because the
  name is the first thing anyone reads when a test fails.

## 11.2 Configuration
All pytest settings live in `[tool.pytest.ini_options]`. There's no `pytest.ini` or `setup.cfg`.
```toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
minversion = "8.0"
testpaths = ["tests"]
addopts = [
    "-ra",                 # summarize skips, xfails, and failures at the end
    "--strict-markers",    # an undeclared marker (e.g. a typo) is an error
    "--strict-config",     # a misspelled setting in this table is an error
    "-m", "not slow",      # deselect slow tests by default
]
markers = [
    "slow: longer-running tests (run with `-m slow`)",
]
xfail_strict = true
filterwarnings = ["error"]
```
- `testpaths` lets `pytest` run from anywhere in the repo, and stops it wandering into `.venv`
  or `docs/`.
- `--strict-markers` and `--strict-config` turn silent typos into errors (already in Great Docs
  and nokap; **new** for the template).
- `xfail_strict = true` **(new)**: an `xfail` test that starts passing is reported as a failure,
  so a fixed bug's marker gets removed and the test goes back to guarding against it.
- `filterwarnings = ["error"]` **(new)**: any warning a test doesn't explicitly expect fails it, so
  deprecation warnings from dependencies are noticed early, not when the removal lands. A warning
  that's known and harmless gets a targeted ignore, scoped by message, category and module, as
  Whittaker already does:
  ```toml
  filterwarnings = [
      "error",
      "ignore:Determining the column names:polars.exceptions.PerformanceWarning:narwhals",
  ]
  ```

## 11.3 Running tests: `make test` and CI
- `make test` runs the suite with coverage and the 10 slowest durations:
  ```make
  test: ## Run the test suite with coverage
  	@$(PYTHON) -m pytest --cov=mypkg --cov-report=term-missing --durations 10
  ```
- In the newest template (Whittaker, GlassDelta) these options are in `addopts` instead. Keeping
  them in the Makefile **(new)** leaves a bare `pytest` fast and uncluttered while iterating,
  with `make test` as the full run. Either way, `make test` is the command people run.
- Companion targets: `make test-update` (accept snapshot changes), `make test-coverage` (list
  only the lines no test runs, via `--cov-report=term-missing:skip-covered`; **new**), plus
  targets for marked subsets where a project has them (`test-unit`, `test-rparity`,
  `test-slow`).
- CI runs `make test` too (with `PYTHON=python` to use the runner's Python instead of `.venv`),
  so "passes locally" and "passes in CI" mean the same thing. See item 12 for the matrix.
- Day-to-day pytest flags: `-x` (stop at first failure), `--lf` (rerun last failures), `-k`
  (select by name), `--pdb` (debugger on failure).

## 11.4 Writing tests
- Plain `assert`, relying on pytest's assertion rewriting to show both sides when a comparison
  fails. No `unittest.TestCase` or `assertEqual`. Test classes are rare: functions are the norm.
- One behavior per test. Several asserts are fine when they check one thing together.
- **Parametrize heavily.** Each case tests one behavior and specifies only the arguments that
  differ from the defaults. Cases get readable ids, either with `ids=` or, better, with
  `pytest.param(..., id="...")` next to each case:
  ```python
  @pytest.mark.parametrize(
      "x, expected",
      [
          pytest.param(0.256, "25.6%", id="typical"),
          pytest.param(1.5, "150.0%", id="over-100"),
      ],
  )
  def test_fmt_percent(x, expected):
      assert fmt_percent(x) == expected
  ```
- **Errors are tested, messages included.** `pytest.raises(..., match=...)` checks the exception
  type and the message. Since good error messages are part of the API (item 21), a test can also
  check that the message names the valid options:
  ```python
  with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="Unknown currency 'XYZ'"):
      fmt_currency(10, currency="XYZ")
  ```
- **Not raising is tested by calling.** Any exception that escapes a test fails it, so a test
  that only needs the call to succeed just makes the call, with a comment saying so. Usually it
  also asserts something about the result. When valid and invalid inputs share one parametrize
  table, the expectation itself is parametrized, with `contextlib.nullcontext` standing in for
  `pytest.raises`:
  ```python
  from contextlib import nullcontext as does_not_raise

  @pytest.mark.parametrize(
      "decimals, expectation",
      [
          pytest.param(2, does_not_raise(), id="two-ok"),
          pytest.param(-1, pytest.raises(ValueError), id="negative-raises"),
      ],
  )
  def test_fmt_number_validates_decimals(decimals, expectation):
      with expectation:
          fmt_number(1.0, decimals=decimals)
  ```
- **Warnings are tested with `pytest.warns`**, which `filterwarnings = ["error"]` makes mandatory
  for code that's meant to warn.
- **Floats are never compared with `==`.** Use `pytest.approx` for scalars and short lists, and
  `numpy.testing.assert_allclose` for arrays. The tolerance should reflect how precise the
  expected value really is; comparisons to zero need an absolute tolerance (`abs=`), because a
  relative one is meaningless there.
- Design decisions get pinned down by tests: keyword-only arguments (item 17), frozen result
  objects (item 19), and deterministic reprs.

## 11.5 Fixtures
- Shared setup is a fixture, never copy-pasted. Fixtures used by several files go in
  `conftest.py`; fixtures used by one file stay in that file.
- Fixtures are function-scoped (rebuilt for every test) by default, which keeps tests
  independent. Expensive, read-only setup, such as fitting a model or loading a large dataset,
  uses `scope="module"` or `scope="session"`, as many of the Whittaker and GlassDelta test files
  do. Never use a broad scope for something a test might modify.
- Fixtures that need cleanup `yield` instead of `return`; the code after `yield` is the teardown.
- Built-in fixtures are used instead of hand-rolled equivalents: `tmp_path` for anything that
  writes files (nothing is ever written into the repo), `monkeypatch` for environment variables
  and attributes, `capsys` for printed output.
- Shared fixtures get a docstring, which `pytest --fixtures` displays.

## 11.6 Markers, skips and xfails
- Every custom marker is declared under `markers`, with a description. Common ones:
  - `slow`: deselected by default with `-m "not slow"`.
  - `integration`: needs something external, such as Chrome (great-tables, nokap); not run in CI.
  - `rparity`: numeric validation against R (see 11.9).
- **Optional dependencies:** `pytest.importorskip("polars")` skips a test when a backend isn't
  installed. Great Tables also has a dedicated `no_pandas` run that proves the package imports
  and works without pandas.
- `@pytest.mark.skipif(condition, reason=...)` for platform- or version-specific tests. Every
  skip has a reason, and `-ra` lists them all in the summary, so skipped tests don't go
  unnoticed.
- `@pytest.mark.xfail(reason=...)` records a known bug or missing feature as a test that's
  expected to fail. With `xfail_strict = true`, fixing the bug forces the marker's removal.

## 11.7 Snapshot tests
- Long rendered output (HTML tables, reports, SVG) is checked with snapshot tests rather than
  hand-written expected strings: **syrupy** (Great Tables) or **pytest-snapshot** (the newest
  template and Pointblank).
- The workflow: write the test, record with `make test-update` (`--snapshot-update`), **read the
  recorded output to confirm it's right**, and commit it with the test. When output changes
  later, the test fails with a diff; if the change is intended, re-record.
- Reviewing the snapshot diff is part of code review. A snapshot only proves the output didn't
  change, not that it's correct, so a recorded snapshot nobody looked at is worthless.
- Snapshots are kept small and focused: snapshot just the part of the output under test (the
  table body, not the whole page), so diffs stay readable and unrelated changes don't break
  unrelated tests.
- HTML snapshots can be stored as standalone `.html` files (a syrupy extension), so they can be
  opened in a browser.
- Snapshot files are excluded from the pre-commit hygiene hooks, which would otherwise "fix" them
  (`end-of-file-fixer` adds a final newline) and break the snapshot tests:
  ```yaml
  exclude: ^tests/__snapshots__/
  ```

## 11.8 Docstring examples
- Docstring examples are Quarto `{python}` cells, not `>>>` doctests (item 25), so pytest doesn't
  run them. The docs build does: Great Docs executes every example, and an example that raises
  an error fails the build. Docs CI therefore catches examples that have stopped working.
- Examples demonstrate usage; they don't replace tests. Behavior an example shows is also
  covered by a test, and examples aren't counted toward coverage.

## 11.9 Parity tests against a reference implementation
- The statistics packages check numeric results against R output stored as fixtures in
  `tests/fixtures/r/`, with tight tolerances (`rtol=atol=1e-9`).
- These tests carry the `rparity` marker and have their own Makefile target, so they can be run
  on their own.

## 11.10 Extra test tooling
These plugins appear in the `dev` extra where they earn their place:
- **pytest-randomly** (Pointblank, Whittaker, GlassDelta) runs tests in a random order and reseeds
  `random` for each test, exposing tests that only pass because of what ran before them. The
  seed is printed at the start of the run; reproduce an ordering with `--randomly-seed=<seed>`.
- **hypothesis** (Pointblank, Whittaker, GlassDelta) for property-based tests: instead
  of a few hand-picked cases, state a property that must hold for all inputs and let Hypothesis
  search for a counterexample:
  ```python
  from hypothesis import given, strategies as st

  @given(st.integers())
  def test_fmt_number_always_has_two_decimals(x):
      assert len(fmt_number(x).rsplit(".", 1)[1]) == 2
  ```
- **pytest-xdist** (Great Docs, Pointblank) runs tests in parallel (`-n auto`) once a
  suite gets slow.
- **pytest-timeout** (nokap, weathervault) fails a test that hangs, for code that drives a
  browser or the network.

## 11.11 Package-level tests
- `test_package.py` checks that `__version__` resolves to a real version (not the `"0.0.0"`
  fallback), and that `set(mypkg.__all__)` equals an explicit set of names. Changing the public
  API then takes a deliberate edit to that test, which shows up in review.

## 11.12 Coverage
- Measured with pytest-cov, configured in `pyproject.toml`:
  ```toml
  [tool.coverage.run]
  source = ["mypkg"]
  branch = true

  [tool.coverage.report]
  show_missing = true
  exclude_also = ["if TYPE_CHECKING:"]
  ```
- Branch coverage is on, so both sides of every `if` count.
- Coverage is a guide to untested code, not a target to game. Missing lines are read as "what
  behavior isn't tested?", and the answer is a test of that behavior, not a test that merely
  executes the line. `# pragma: no cover` is reserved for lines that genuinely can't run under
  test, like the `PackageNotFoundError` fallback for `__version__`.
